image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Tile-based cartogram / grid map** of U.S. states.
- Each small square represents **one House seat**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses a **geographic-like grid/cartogram layout** where each state is shown as a cluster of equal-sized tiles.
- **No faceting** or small multiples.
- Not stacked in the chart-type sense; instead, tiles are **grouped by state**.
- Uses **color coding** to distinguish seat change categories.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Grouped tile cluster position in the U.S.-like layout; state text labels |
| Number of House seats | Quantitative | Count of equal-sized tiles (area via repeated unit squares) within each state |
| Seat change status (gaining / losing / no change) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of tiles (green, yellow, light gray) |
| Net seat change value (e.g., +1, -1, +2) | Quantitative | Text labels placed on selected states |

comments.raw_comment:
Is the Wind of Change coming?
Internal migration is occurring in the United States due to several factors. To begin with, we have the Covid-19 economic crisis unleashed in 2020, from which we haven't yet fully recovered. In most cases, due to the high cost of living and taxes in the majority of the states in yellow.

In addition, another critical aspect that has promoted the massive migration in the last year is the environmental crisis that states like California have experienced, where fires and high temperatures are becoming more and more extreme due to climate change.

Most of the states that lost their seats are Democrats, which may obstruct their presence in the House of Representatives. However, as most of the populations that migrated were from Democratic territories, and in that way, it would not be surprising that there will be a change in the popular vote for the next elections in states such as Texas, Florida, North Carolina, and Montana. 

Although most of these green territories have a strong influence from the Republican party, the migration that seems to have occurred in the majority of the Democratic states could change those states from red to blue in the coming years, since migration due to climate change is just beginning. So, is the wind of change coming?

On the other hand, this change will significantly benefit the states that have won electoral seats since it will substantially increase the investment funds in these states.

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  "Shifts in Population = Shifts in Seats? " by Alina and Matthew of Eleanor Roosevelt High School in New York, “New Population Calls for a Change of Seats” by Sarah of Louisiana, “-1 States, +2 States, Red States, Blue States” by Wyatt of Hawaii, "Hey, Where Did My Seat Go?" by Brayden of Indiana, "Change is Power in the Hour of Need" by Jordan, Azhley, and Diego of Chico, California and "2020 Census Causes Congressional Shift" By Lula.
 
 
You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, October 29 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a Stat Nugget.
 
Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex). 
 
Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, whose state almost lost a House of Representatives seat but was “saved” by an increase in residents in high-tech and biological science jobs, and Kevin DeVizia of Millrift, Pennsylvania, who loves contributing to ensuring the fair and accurate election process in his County of Pike, Pennsylvania, and seeing every American having their due opportunity to have a voice in the democratic process.

comments.raw_comment: This graph shows the increase and decrease of seats in the House of Representatives. Something that I noticed is that there is an equivalent balance between the number of members lost and then gained. This is because there should be 435 members divided among 50 states so there should never be more states gaining members without states also losing members. Something I also noticed is that the states that were affected by this change were decently sized states. Also, most of the more populated states like California and New York lost seats. Compared to less populated states like Montana and Oregon gaining seats. I wonder how much this affects the House. I also am curious as to how a state gets to gain members or how they lose members. This relates to my community because while other states are gaining or losing representatives, my state stayed the same. The House of Representatives also affects everyone in the U.S. so even though my state did not have an impact on this change, it still affects me. A catchy headline is "Is Your States Amount of House of Representatives Increasing or Decreasing?"

comments.raw_comment: This graph depicts the changes in the seats in the House of Representatives for each state after the 2020 census. One reason for this could be because of the amount of people that left cities such as Los Angeles and New York City due to fear of the pandemic. I wonder why the population in Texas has increased so much that it receives two extra seats now. I also notice how all of the states that lost seats (except CA) are all in close proximity to each other, meaning the population decrease was widespread over that area. My title for this graph would be: “Congressional Seat Changes in 2020”

Welcome to Wednesday's line moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows the reallocation of House of Representative seats based on the 2020 U.S. Census.  Why is the country’s population shifting and how will be this affect the United States?   

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you and your community?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, October 29 with moderation on Wednesday, November 3.  The topic:  how to reach net-zero emissions in the U.S. by 2050 with wind and solar power.  Keep noticing and wondering!

In this graph, I notice that the population of states that typically have lower populations is increasing. For states with historically higher populations, their population is decreasing. The population in this graph is measured, not by how many people are now living in the states, but by how many seats the state gained/lost in the House of Representatives. Even though the graph does not say exactly how many people now live in the state as compared to previous times, a change in the states' seats in the House is an indicator in a change in the population. 
I wonder if the pandemic has had any role in this shift. In the graph, the population of Texas and Florida increased. Since these two states have had notably lenient COVID-19 protocols in the pandemic, I wonder if people are relocating to these states where there is less regulation for COVID-19. 
This relates to me and my community because the town that I live in is discussing rearranging the public school system arrangement so they can better fit the children in our town. 
A Change in Congressional Seats

Could that have been related to the fact that they were part of the 13 colonies? Does that change the number of seats they should have in the first place? The main thing that I wonder is how much of a population change a state must have to gain or lose a representative seat.    New York: lost seats and state with the highest number of COVID cases and deaths. 

Have other states within the United States not experienced population shifts in the last year?

   Relocation or change in settlement: from bigger to less-populated states during 2020. Could be pandemic-related and/or economically related.
